danish.title: Tiende bog (1812) — Kapitel 35
paragraphs: På den tæppedækkede bænk, hvor Pierre havde set ham om morgenen, sad Kutuzov (fyrst Kutuzov) med sit grå hoved hængende og sin tunge krop slapt. Han gav ingen ordrer, men nøjedes med at bifalde eller forkaste, hvad andre foreslog.

»Ja, ja, gør det,« svarede han på de forskellige forslag. »Ja, ja, kære ven, gå du hen og se efter,« kunne han sige til en af dem omkring sig, eller: »Nej, lad være, vi må hellere vente.« Han hørte på meldingerne og gav anvisninger, når hans underordnede bad ham om det. Men når han lyttede, var det, som om det, der optog ham, var noget andet end ordenes betydning: ansigtsudtrykket og tonefaldet hos den, der afgav meldingen. Af mange års krigserfaring vidste han, og med alderens visdom forstod han, at ét menneske umuligt kan lede hundredtusinder, der kæmper med døden. Han vidste, at udfaldet af et slag hverken afgøres af den øverstkommanderendes ordrer, af hvor tropperne står, eller af hvor mange kanoner eller faldne man tæller, men af den uhåndgribelige kraft, man kalder hærens ånd. Den kraft holdt han øje med og ledede, så vidt det stod i hans magt.
Kutuzovs generelle udtryk var et af samlet, rolig opmærksomhed, og hans ansigt bar et anstrengt præg, som om han fandt det svært at mestre sin gamle, svækkede krops træthed.
Klokken elleve bragte man ham nyheden om, at de flècher, franskmændene havde erobret, var generobret, men at fyrst Bagration var såret. Kutuzov stønnede og rokkede med hovedet.
»Rid over til fyrst Pjotr Ivanovitj og find ud af det præcise,« sagde han til en af sine adjudanter og vendte sig derefter til Hertugen af Württemberg, der stod bag ham.
»Vil Deres Højhed overtage kommandoen over den første armé?«
Kort efter hertugens afgang — før han overhovedet kunne have nået Semjonovsk — kom hans adjudant tilbage og meddelte Kutuzov, at hertugen bad om flere tropper.

Kutuzov lavede en grimasse og sendte ordre til Dokhturov om at overtage kommandoen over den første armé, med en anmodning til hertugen — som han sagde, han ikke kunne undvære i et så vigtigt øjeblik — om at vende tilbage til ham. Da de bragte ham nyheden om, at Murat var taget til fange, og stabsofficererne lykønskede ham, smilede Kutuzov.
»Vent lidt, mine herrer,« sagde han. »Slaget er vundet, og der er intet usædvanligt i tilfangetagelsen af Murat. Men det er bedre at vente, før vi jubler.«
Men han sendte dog en adjudant ud for at bringe nyheden rundt i hæren.

Da Sjerbinin kom galoperende fra venstre fløj med nyheden om, at franskmændene havde erobret flècherne og landsbyen Semjonovsk, rejste Kutuzov sig, idet han gættede af slagets lyde og af Sjerbinins udtryk, at nyheden var dårlig — rejste sig, som for at strække benene, tog Sjerbinins arm og førte ham til side.
»Gå, min kære ven,« sagde han til Jermolóv (general Jermolóv), »og se, om der ikke kan gøres noget.«

Kutuzov var i Gorki, nær centrum af den russiske stilling. Det franske angreb mod den russiske venstre fløj var blevet slået tilbage flere gange. I centrum var franskmændene ikke nået længere end Borodino, og på deres venstre fløj havde Uvarovs kavaleri slået franskmændene på flugt.

Hen imod klokken tre hørte de franske angreb op. I ansigterne på alle, der kom fra slagmarken, og dem, der stod omkring ham, bemærkede Kutuzov et udtryk af ekstrem anspændthed. Han var tilfreds med dagens resultat — en succes, der oversteg hans forventninger — men den gamle mands kræfter svigtede ham. Hans hoved sank, og han nikkede med. Der blev sat frokost frem til ham.

Generaladjudant Wolzogen, den mand, der, da han red forbi fyrst Andrej, havde sagt, at »krigen bør udvides bredt,« og som Bagration afskyede så dybt, red op, mens Kutuzov spiste frokost. Wolzogen var kommet fra Barclay de Tolly for at rapportere om tingenes tilstand på venstre fløj. Den kloge Barclay de Tolly, der så flokke af sårede løbe tilbage, og baglinjens uorden, vejede alle omstændigheder og konkluderede, at slaget var tabt, og sendte sin yndling til øverstkommanderende med denne besked.
Kutuzov tyggede på et stykke stegt kylling med besvær og kiggede på Wolzogen med øjne, der lyste under de rynkede øjenlåg.
Wolzogen nærmede sig Kutuzov med en halvt foragtelig nonchalance, mens han let berørte toppen af sin hue og strakte sine ben ud.

Han behandlede Hans Durchlaucht med en noget påtaget ligegyldighed, der skulle vise, at han som højtdannet militærmand overlod det til russerne at gøre en afgud af denne uduelige gamle mand, men at han selv godt vidste, hvem han havde med at gøre. »Der alte Herr« (som tyskerne i deres egen kreds kaldte Kutuzov) »gør sig det nemt,« tænkte Wolzogen, og med et strengt blik på de tallerkener, der stod foran Kutuzov, begyndte han at rapportere til »den gamle herre« om situationen på venstre fløj, som Barclay havde bedømt den.
»Alle punkter i vores stilling er i fjendens hænder, og vi kan ikke drive dem ud, fordi vi mangler tropper, mændene flygter, og det er umuligt at standse dem,« rapporterede han.
Kutuzov holdt op med at tygge og fæstnede et forbavset blik på Wolzogen, som om han ikke forstod, hvad der blev sagt til ham. Wolzogen, der bemærkede »den gamle herres« ophidselse, sagde med et smil:
»Jeg har ikke anset det for rigtigt at skjule for Deres Durchlaucht, hvad jeg har set. Tropperne er i fuldstændig opløsning...«
»De har set? De har set?...« råbte Kutuzov. Med rynket pande rejste han sig hurtigt og gik hen mod Wolzogen.

»Hvordan... hvordan vover De!...« råbte han og kvaltes, mens han truede med sine rystende arme: »Hvordan vover De, min herre, at sige det til mig? De ved ingenting om det. Sig til general Barclay fra mig, at hans oplysninger er forkerte, og at den virkelige gang i slaget er bedre kendt af mig — øverstkommanderende — end af ham.«
Wolzogen ville svare, men Kutuzov afbrød ham.

»Fjenden er slået tilbage på venstre fløj og besejret på højre fløj. Hvis De har set fejl, min herre, så tillad Dem ikke at sige, hvad De ikke ved! Vær så venlig at ride til general Barclay og meddele ham min faste hensigt at angribe fjenden i morgen,« sagde Kutuzov strengt.
Alle var tavse, og den eneste lyd var den stønnende gamle generals tunge åndedrag.

»De er slået tilbage overalt, og jeg takker Gud og vor tapre hær for det! Fjenden er besejret, og i morgen skal vi drive ham fra Ruslands hellige jord,« sagde Kutuzov og korsede sig, og pludselig hulkede han, da hans øjne fyldtes med tårer.
Wolzogen trak på skuldrene, krusede læberne og trådte tavst til side, forundret over »den gamle herres« indbildske dumhed.
»Ah, dér er han, min helt!« sagde Kutuzov til en kraftig, flot, mørkhåret general, der netop var på vej op ad bakken.
Det var Rajevskij, der havde tilbragt hele dagen ved slagets vigtigste punkt på Borodino-slagmarken.
Rajevskij rapporterede, at tropperne holdt deres stillinger fast, og at franskmændene ikke længere vovede at angribe.
Efter at have hørt ham sagde Kutuzov på fransk:
»Så De mener ikke, som visse andre, at vi er nødt til at trække os tilbage?«
»Tværtimod, Deres Højhed — i uafgjorte slag er det altid den mest hårdnakkede, der sejrer,« svarede Rajevskij, »og efter min mening...«
»Kajsarov!« kaldte Kutuzov sin adjudant. »Sæt dig og skriv dagsordren for i morgen. Og De,« fortsatte han til en anden, »rid langs linjen og meddel, at vi angriber i morgen.«
Mens Kutuzov talte med Rajevskij og dikterede dagsordren, vendte Wolzogen tilbage fra Barclay og sagde, at general Barclay ønskede skriftlig bekræftelse af den ordre, feltmarskalken havde givet.
Kutuzov, uden at se på Wolzogen, beordrede ordren skrevet ud — ordren, som den forhenværende øverstkommanderende, for at undgå personligt ansvar, meget fornuftigt ønskede at modtage skriftligt.

Og i kraft af det mystiske, udefinerlige bånd, der gennemsyrer en hel hær og opretholder én og samme stemning — kendt som »hærens ånd« — og som udgør krigens nerve, blev Kutuzovs ord, hans ordre om slag den næste dag, øjeblikkeligt kendt fra den ene ende af hæren til den anden.

Det var langtfra de samme ord eller den samme ordre, der nåede til de fjerneste led i den kæde. De historier, der gik fra mund til mund i hærens forskellige afkroge, lignede ikke engang, hvad Kutuzov havde sagt, men meningen med hans ord bredte sig overalt — for hvad han sagde var ikke resultatet af kløgtige beregninger, men udsprang af en følelse, der lå i øverstkommanderendes sjæl, ligesom i hver eneste russisk soldats sjæl.
Og da de hørte, at de næste dag skulle angribe fjenden, og da de fra de højeste kredse fik bekræftet det, de ønskede at tro, følte de udmattede, vaklende mænd sig trøstede og opildnede.

english.title: Book Ten (1812) — Chapter 35
paragraphs: On the rug-covered bench where Pierre had seen him that morning, Kutuzov sat with his gray head hanging, his heavy body relaxed. He gave no orders — he merely agreed with or overruled what others suggested.

"Yes, yes, do that," he replied to various proposals. "Yes, yes — go, my dear fellow, and have a look," he would say to one or another around him; or, "No, don't — we'd better wait!" He listened to reports and gave directions when his subordinates required them; but while listening, he seemed less interested in the substance of the words than in the expressions and tones of voice of those reporting. Through long years of military experience, he knew — and with the wisdom of age understood — that no single man can direct hundreds of thousands of others locked in a struggle with death, and that the outcome of a battle is decided not by a commander's orders, nor by troop positions, nor by the number of cannons or dead, but by that intangible force called the spirit of the army. He watched that spirit and guided it as best he could.
Kutuzov's general expression was one of concentrated quiet attention, his face strained, as though the fatigue of his old, feeble body was hard to endure.
At eleven o'clock they brought him news that the fortifications captured by the French had been retaken, but that Prince Bagration was wounded. Kutuzov groaned and shook his head.
"Ride over to Prince Peter Ivanovich and find out exactly what's happened," he said to one of his adjutants, then turned to the Duke of Wurttemberg standing behind him.
"Will Your Highness please take command of the First Army?"
Soon after the Duke's departure — before he could possibly have reached Semenovsk — his adjutant returned and told Kutuzov that the Duke was requesting more troops.

Kutuzov grimaced and sent an order for Dokhturov to take command of the First Army, and a request to the Duke — whom he said he couldn't spare at such a critical moment — to return. When they brought news that Murat had been taken prisoner and the staff officers congratulated him, Kutuzov smiled.
"Wait a moment, gentlemen," he said. "The battle is won, and there's nothing extraordinary about capturing Murat. Still, it's better to hold off on celebrations."
But he sent an adjutant to carry the news through the army.

When Shcherbinin came galloping from the left flank with news that the French had captured the fortifications and the village of Semenovsk, Kutuzov — guessing from the sounds of battle and Shcherbinin's expression that the news was bad — stood up as if to stretch his legs and, taking Shcherbinin's arm, led him aside.
"Go, my dear fellow," he said to Ermolov, "and see if something can't be done."

Kutuzov was at Gorki, near the center of the Russian position. The attack Napoleon had directed against the Russian left flank had been repulsed several times. In the center the French had not advanced beyond Borodino, and on their left flank Uvarov's cavalry had routed the French.

Toward three o'clock the French attacks stopped. On the faces of everyone coming from the battlefield and those around him, Kutuzov noticed an expression of extreme tension. He was satisfied with the day's success — which exceeded his expectations — but the old man's strength was failing. Several times his head drooped as if falling, and he dozed off. Dinner was brought to him.

Adjutant General Wolzogen, the man who had told Prince Andrew in passing that "the war should be extended widely" and whom Bagration had so despised, rode up while Kutuzov was eating. Wolzogen came from Barclay de Tolly to report on affairs on the left flank. The shrewd Barclay, seeing crowds of wounded streaming back and the army's rear in disorder, had weighed all the circumstances, concluded the battle was lost, and sent his favorite officer to the commander in chief with that news.
Kutuzov was chewing a piece of roast chicken with difficulty and glanced at Wolzogen with eyes that brightened under their puckered lids.
Wolzogen, casually stretching out his legs, approached Kutuzov with a half-contemptuous smile, barely touching the peak of his cap.

He treated his Serene Highness with a somewhat affected indifference intended to show that, as a highly trained military man, he left it to the Russians to make an idol of this useless old man, while he himself knew exactly who he was dealing with. "The old gentleman" — as the Germans in their circle called Kutuzov — "is making himself very comfortable," Wolzogen thought, and looking critically at the dishes before Kutuzov, he began reporting the situation on the left flank as Barclay had instructed him and as he himself had observed.
"All our positions are in the enemy's hands and we can't dislodge them because there aren't enough troops. The men are running away and it's impossible to stop them," he reported.
Kutuzov stopped chewing and stared at Wolzogen in astonishment, as if not understanding what was being said. Wolzogen, noticing the old man's agitation, said with a smile:
"I did not consider it right to hide from your Serene Highness what I have seen. The troops are in complete disorder..."
"You have seen? You have seen?" Kutuzov shouted. Scowling and rising quickly, he went up to Wolzogen.

"How... how dare you!" he choked, making a threatening gesture with his trembling arms. "How dare you, sir, say that to me? You know nothing about it. Tell General Barclay from me that his information is incorrect and that the real course of the battle is better known to me, the commander in chief, than to him."
Wolzogen was about to reply, but Kutuzov cut him off.

"The enemy has been repulsed on the left and defeated on the right flank. If you have seen poorly, sir, do not allow yourself to state what you don't know! Be so good as to ride to General Barclay and inform him of my firm intention to attack the enemy tomorrow," Kutuzov said sternly.
Everyone fell silent, and the only sound was the heavy breathing of the panting old general.

"They are repulsed everywhere, for which I thank God and our brave army! The enemy is beaten, and tomorrow we shall drive him from the sacred soil of Russia," said Kutuzov, crossing himself, and he suddenly sobbed as his eyes filled with tears.
Wolzogen shrugged, curled his lips, and stepped silently aside, marveling at "the old gentleman's" conceited stupidity.
"Ah, here he is, my hero!" said Kutuzov to a stocky, handsome, dark-haired general who was just climbing the knoll.
This was Raevsky, who had spent the whole day at the most critical part of the Borodino field.
Raevsky reported that the troops were firmly holding their ground and that the French no longer dared to attack.
After hearing him, Kutuzov said in French:
"Then you don't think, like some others, that we must retreat?"
"On the contrary, your Highness — in indecisive battles it is always the most stubborn side that wins," replied Raevsky, "and in my opinion..."

"Kaisarov!" Kutuzov called to his adjutant. "Sit down and write out the order of the day for tomorrow. And you," he continued, turning to another officer, "ride along the line and announce that tomorrow we attack."
While Kutuzov was talking to Raevsky and dictating the order of the day, Wolzogen returned from Barclay and said that the general wanted written confirmation of the order the field marshal had given.

Kutuzov, without looking at Wolzogen, gave instructions for the order to be written out — an order that the former commander in chief, to avoid personal responsibility, very shrewdly wanted in writing.

And through that mysterious, indefinable bond that maintains the same spirit throughout an army — known as "the spirit of the army" and constituting the sinew of war — Kutuzov's words and his order for battle the next day immediately became known from one end of the army to the other.

It was far from the same words or the same order that reached the farthest links of that chain. The stories passing from mouth to mouth bore little resemblance to what Kutuzov had actually said, but the meaning of his words spread everywhere because what he said was not the product of cunning calculation but of a feeling that lay in the commander in chief's soul — as it lay in the soul of every Russian.
And when the exhausted, wavering men learned they were to attack the enemy tomorrow, and heard from the highest command confirmation of what they wanted to believe, they felt comforted and inspired.
